scope: One additional adult angelfish for the existing species guide, optional identification activity and illustrative reef encounters. The model represents a Pacific individual; regional colour forms are explained rather than blended. New copy is paraphrased from museum accounts and primary research. Model-based field marks support learning, not guaranteed field identification.
iucnYearConvention: Use assessment year 2009, not publication year 2010. The current indexed FishBase IUCN 2025-2 export reports Least Concern with assessment date 8 October 2009. IUCN-owned Crossref metadata gives the same date; Museums Victoria cites the 2010 Red List publication. Direct IUCN access returned 403, so no successful direct Red List-page access is claimed.

specimens.name: Regal angelfish
marks: Pale, dark-edged vertical bars cross a yellow-orange body
The soft rear dorsal fin is blue with fine dark scribbles
The anal fin carries curved yellow and blue stripes
A yellow tail contrasts with the blue-grey chest of this Pacific adult
specimens.role: Predator of sponges and tunicates, linking these reef invertebrates to the fish food web.
specimens.fact: Colour varies geographically: Indian Ocean and Red Sea fish have yellow chests, while the Pacific form shown here has a blue-grey chest.
specimens.habitat: Coral-rich lagoons and seaward reefs, often around caves and ledges. The species ranges from East Africa and the Red Sea across the tropical Indo-Pacific to the Tuamotu region.
specimens.diet: Feeds on sponges and tunicates, including sea squirts.
specimens.behavior: Usually encountered alone or in pairs, occasionally in small groups. Young fish shelter in coral cracks and crevices.
specimens.observe: Follow the bars down this adult’s sides, then compare the emperor angelfish’s finer, mostly horizontal stripes. Check the tail, fin patterns and chest colour together; juveniles and regional forms differ.

claimSupport.acceptedName: dx-cas-regal_angelfish: current accepted name is Pygoplites diacanthus (Boddaert, 1772).
claimSupport.marks: dx-am-regal_angelfish supports alternating pale, black-edged bars, blue dorsal with dark scribbles, striped anal fin and yellow tail; dx-foa-regal_angelfish supports the orange-yellow ground colour and head/side bars; dx-phylogeography-regal_angelfish supports the Pacific grey chest and head.
claimSupport.roleDiet: dx-foa-regal_angelfish and dx-am-regal_angelfish identify sponges and tunicates as food. The food-web wording is a conservative interpretation of feeding, not a claim of measured ecosystem control.
claimSupport.fact: dx-phylogeography-regal_angelfish: introduction and Figure 1 explicitly contrast yellow-chested Indian Ocean/Red Sea fish with grey-chested Pacific fish, illustrated by Djibouti and Great Barrier Reef individuals.
claimSupport.habitatRange: dx-am-regal_angelfish and dx-foa-regal_angelfish: coral-rich lagoons and seaward reefs, caves and ledges; broad Indo-West-Central Pacific distribution.
claimSupport.behavior: dx-am-regal_angelfish and dx-foa-regal_angelfish: solitary, paired or occasionally small-group encounters; juveniles shelter in crevices.
claimSupport.compare: dx-usgs-emperor-regal_angelfish describes adult emperor angelfish flank striping and explicitly identifies it as horizontal in its comparison section. The existing emperor record is linked one-way without changing its copy.
claimSupport.iucn: dx-iucn-regal_angelfish gives the IUCN assessment DOI and 2010 publication; IUCN-owned Crossref metadata and dx-fb-regal_angelfish corroborate 8 October 2009 as the assessment date; the current FishBase IUCN 2025-2 export retains LC.
claimSupport.sizeDepth: dx-foa-regal_angelfish gives maximum 25 cm total length and depths 1–80 m. dx-am-regal_angelfish gives 25 cm and 1–48 m. The broader museum interval is used for encounter metadata, with source differences retained in provenance.

specimens.caution: The geographic chest colours describe adult regional forms, not an infallible geographic or taxonomic identification rule. Coleman et al. (2016) documented genetic partitions and discussed subspecies; the current 2026 Eschmeyer catalog retains P. diacanthus as valid and notes that the Indian/Red Sea name flavescens was misapplied. No subspecies name is assigned here. Juveniles have a dorsal eyespot and different proportions/colouring; that eyespot is not added to this adult. Fin rays, exact bar counts and natural colour variation are simplified. LC is a global assessment, not a statement that every local population or reef habitat is secure. No aquarium hardiness, reef-safety, camouflage mechanism or ecosystem-control claim is imported.

modelProvenance.representative: Pacific / Great Barrier Reef adult with a blue-grey chest and reduced yellow on the head. Do not blend the yellow-chested Indian Ocean/Red Sea form into this individual.
modelProvenance.basis: Illustrative 20 cm adult below the museum-reported 25 cm maximum. The 1–80 m encounter interval follows Fishes of Australia; the Australian Museum gives 1–48 m. Neither interval is treated as a physiological limit or a promise of encounter frequency at every depth.
modelProvenance.anatomy: Laterally compressed adult angelfish silhouette with a small mouth and preopercular spine. Yellow-orange body crossed by pale, dark-edged bars; grey-blue lower head and chest; blue soft dorsal with dark scribbles; curved yellow/blue anal-fin stripes; yellow caudal fin. Adult only, without a juvenile dorsal ocellus.
modelProvenance.anatomyLimits: Exact ray and bar counts, individual variation and fine scale detail are simplified. The chosen regional colour form is explicit; neither colour nor the simplified model alone establishes definitive wild identification or a formal subspecies.
modelProvenance.motion: Gentle pectoral-fin adjustments and restrained body/tail movement for reef manoeuvring. Solitary or paired illustrative encounters fit the museum account better than a dense coordinated school; timings are artistic, not measured swimming data.

integration.lookalikeNote: Link one-way to the existing adult emperor angelfish to teach mostly vertical bars versus finer horizontal striping. Preserve the emperor record exactly. Both are adult-model comparisons; juveniles differ.
